On Ramchandra Ray’s escape night, Udayaditya dominates Sitaram: he orders him to open the door, threatens him with his sword, and then disarms and binds him when Sitaram submits. On Udayaditya’s own escape night, the roles reverse: Sitaram enters as the active rescuer, grabs and nearly carries Udayaditya out, and leads him, while Udayaditya is helpless and asks where to go.

Pratapaditya’s first plan was to have two Pathan men kill Basanta Ray at the inn in Simultali on his way to Jessore, but it failed when the Pathan did not carry it out. The old king was finally killed by execution under Pratapaditya’s signed death order: Muktiyar Khan had Abdul come in with a drawn sword, and Basanta Ray was cut down, leaving the sword bloodied.
In the Jessore palace inner quarters, disguised as a woman, and in the royal palace room, in his jester’s role/guise.
Mangala (Rukmini) secretly prepares a poison, and it is covertly given to Surma, causing her to die.
The Maharaj of Chandradwip takes revenge by marrying another, leaving no place for Vibha in his own palace; she is turned away and denied forgiveness.

Rukminī takes Udayaditya’s ring, which bears the Yubaraj’s seal; Sitāram and Bhāgavat then use that seal to stamp a forged petition, and Bhāgavat delivers the sealed petition to Pratāpadya. The ring’s seal makes the forged petition look authentic, and it is used as evidence for Udayaditya’s imprisonment.

Ramchandra Ray’s midnight escape led to Udayaditya’s later support of the dismissed guards Sitaram and Bhagavat with monthly stipends; when Pratapaditya learned of this, he took it as Udayaditya’s defiance and ordered Surma to be sent to her father’s home.

The song expresses Basanta Ray’s profound loneliness and grief: it declares that everything he once had has gone away, leaving only emptiness, and that those who were once his no longer answer him, making him feel unable to go on living without that lost joy and connection.

He sings it in two contrasting contexts: first, alone on the palace veranda in Raigarh at sunset, humming it to himself in private reflection before the full news of Udayaditya’s imprisonment is delivered; and second, in Jessore, in the dark, silent, empty room of the household after he has learned of Udayaditya’s imprisonment, taking Vibha’s hand and singing it in a heart-rending voice amid the actual desolation and absence of his loved ones.

Rukmini’s failed attempt to stop Udayaditya’s escape led to her disclosing to Pratapaditya that Udayaditya had fled with Basanta Ray; this disclosure led to the king issuing a death order for Basanta Ray, which was carried out by Muktiyar Khan and Abdul, killing Basanta Ray.

Pratapaditya initially received Ramchandra Ray with quiet, formal restraint—without ceremonial fanfare—greeted him calmly, handled ministerial business, and treated him with dignified superiority. In contrast, Ramchandra later addresses Pratapaditya’s status in his own court by mocking and belittling him, using jests about his lineage and asserting that his own house is far greater and that the marriage only brought merit to Pratapaditya.

Rukmini, now called Mangala, re-enters Udayaditya’s life by leaving Raigarh and moving to the outskirts of Jessore, befriending palace servants, and using her knowledge of tantra, mantra, and medicine to prepare a poison that leads to Surma’s death.

Udayaditya’s early private lament—his wish not to be born a crown prince and his sense that he is unfit and unwanted—culminates in a public, sworn renunciation. After being brought before Pratapaditya as a prisoner, he declares that he is not worthy of the kingdom and asks for release. He then takes an oath before Ma-Kali, with Pratapaditya present, swearing that as long as he lives he will never accept even an iota of Jessore’s kingdom, will not sit on its throne, and will not touch its royal scepter, while confirming Samaraditya as the heir.

The letter was intercepted by the old Nayanchand, to whom Ramchandra Ray had entrusted its delivery to Jessore. Fearing what Pratapaditya might do if the letter reached him, Nayanchand did not deliver it and instead handed it to the Mahishi.

The Mahishi then misrepresented it to Vibha through Basanta Ray's simple-minded misreading of the letter. Basanta Ray believed the letter was written only out of anger and that sending Vibha back would end it. On his advice, the Mahishi announced to Vibha and throughout the household that Ramchandra Ray had written a letter *requesting* that Vibha be sent to Chandradwip — inverting the letter's actual content, which stated that he had renounced her and she should not be sent there again. Vibha took this as confirmation that her husband was not abandoning her.
Rammohan and his followers pulled the boat up and over the logs that had blocked the canal.

Basanta Ray’s sitar, once his “eternal companion,” becomes a symbol of his broken inner joy. He leaves it behind saying he will not play it anymore, and later claims its strings are broken and it can no longer be tuned. His inability to resume playing it—even while he can still join another’s song briefly—shows that Udayaditya’s imprisonment has emptied his musical life of its purpose and companionship, turning the sitar into an emblem of his growing despair.

Earlier, Udayaditya was bold and willing to risk consequences to intervene on behalf of oppressed subjects—stopping officials and protecting them even against his king. After Surma’s death, his former courage is gone; fear of Pratapaditya makes him hesitant, so he no longer intervenes, helps the distressed, or acts against injustice.
He rescues Udayaditya from the prison during the fire, carrying him out into the open.

On one desperate occasion, Rammohan ties thick sheets together into a rope, carries Ramchandra Ray on his back, and lowers him from the palace roof into the boat. On the other, he lifts the fainted Vibha, carries her out of the palace, and places her in a palanquin near the gate.

In Jessore, Vibha is lavishly dressed by her mother-in-law—thick gold bangles and a huge diamond bracelet on each arm, a large nose ring, and an elaborate hairstyle—and is presented with shy, flustered joy. In Chandradwip, she instead presents herself plainly as a common woman, even like a beggar-woman, without a palanquin, her veil fallen, entering like an ordinary maidservant and humbling herself at the king’s feet.

After Surma's death, the window in Udayaditya’s bedchamber symbolizes absence and grief: it is the place where Surma used to sit, and he sits there looking at the same moonlight, garden, and breeze, waiting for her and feeling her loss.

In the prison cell, the window changes into a symbol of freedom and hope: through it he can see the sky and birds, and he imagines his cage breaking. When he is away from the window, he sees only darkness and forgets that he will one day be liberated; the window becomes the spot where he feels naturally free.

The devolution proceeds in distinct stages:

**Flirtatious financial arrangement.** Sitaram, a stylish but penniless man, has a "sincere attraction" to both Rukmini's beauty and her silver. He borrows money from her, claiming his mother has his money and that he will pay it back tomorrow, while Rukmini feigns affection and tells him he can repay "whenever it's convenient." Sitaram plays the nawab and the wit, making grand pronouncements, calling her "Subhadra," "Pran," "Priye," "Priyatame," and "Pranpriye," and jokingly asking what interest she will charge. Rukmini teases and pouts, but the exchange remains playful and reciprocal, with Sitaram treating the money as free and both parties engaged in witty banter.

**Shift to secrecy and conspiracy.** Sitaram begins visiting Rukmini frequently, and they are seen "conferring together on some matter in great secrecy." Sitaram admits he is "not that good at scheming" and says he will need Bhagavat's help, indicating the relationship has moved from casual flirtation to involvement in a plot concerning Udayaditya.

**Confrontation and threat over Udayaditya's imprisonment.** When Sitaram learns Udayaditya has been imprisoned, he is "beside himself." He goes to Rukmini's house and curses her with whatever comes to mind, all but striking her, threatening to set her house on fire, free the Yubaraj, and after returning from Raigarh, to "grind that wretched face of yours on this stone floor," smear her face with lime and soot, and drive her from the city. Rukmini's reaction is one of "demonic curse, a trembling hatred that swelled through her entire body"—her teeth clench, fists tighten, lightning collects in her pupils, and she asserts that Udayaditya is *her* Yubaraj, and that only she can do him good or harm. The flirtatious arrangement has become openly adversarial.

**Sitaram's planned robbery.** After the fire at Udayaditya's prison, Sitaram returns to the city and, while heading to his cottage, thinks: "That wretched Mangala is dead—good riddance—let me just stop by her house. The bitch has a lot of money... if I don't take the money, someone else will. So what's the harm, let me give it a try!" He enters her cottage with the intent to steal.

**The life-threatening encounter.** Inside the dark cottage, Sitaram trips over a chest, bumps his head, and feels a "creepy feeling" as if someone is in the room. He sees Rukmini sitting in the faint light, disheveled, with a wet cloth around her body, water dripping from her hair, teeth chattering, trembling violently. He thinks she is a ghost and, in a tone of "feigned courage and verbal mockery," calls her "wench, are you immortal or what!" Rukmini stares fixedly at him, and his heart pounds. She then stands up and waves her hand, saying: "I have returned from the door of Yama! First, I will lay you and the Yubaraj in the oven, and only after I have smeared my body with two handfuls of ash from your pyres to consecrate my body—will I satisfy Yama's desire—before that, there is no place for me in Yamalaya." This is an explicit death threat directed at Sitaram.

**Rage and the blade.** Sitaram tries to "feign great affection and make up with Rukmini," calling her soft names and asking if she is sulking. But "the more Sitaram feigned affection, the more enraged Rukmini became—her entire body, from head to foot, burned with rage." She says, "Just you wait; I'm going to make you pay," and trembles violently as she goes into the next room "in search of a curved blade." Sitaram, having made a metaphorical proposal to die earlier but now "realized that he was not yet ready to die from the blow of a real blade," seizes the opportunity and "immediately slipped out of the cottage." Rukmini, "blade in hand," comes into the empty room and "repeatedly struck the floor where Sitaram had stood."

**Aftermath.** Rukmini has become reckless and dangerous—her "sharp, honed smile" and "electrifying side-glance" are gone, she has driven away palace servants, chased off the Dewanji's eldest son with a broom, and "everyone in the neighborhood was afraid of her." Sitaram, upon leaving, thinks: "Mangala knows everything about the Yubaraj's escape... why didn't I just strangle the wretch to death!" He then flees Jessore with his family to Raigarh, while Rukmini is later brought before the king, who orders men to be sent to find those responsible for Udayaditya's escape and the fire.

Sitaram first uses the guardhouse/palace fire as a diversion: he allows or arranges a blaze that creates panic, prevents the guards from maintaining order, and gives him an urgent pretext to enter Udayaditya’s prison and take him out under the claim that the prison itself is on fire. The plan then becomes a full cover-up of the escape: after Udayaditya is removed, Sitaram’s men set fire to his empty prison cell, and Sitaram plants bones, a skull, and the Yubaraj’s sword inside the room. When the cell fire becomes intense and the roof collapses, he announces that there is no response from Udayaditya, leading the guards to argue and accept that the Yubaraj died in the fire. Court testimony about screams, the Yubaraj being seen, and a burnt sword is then produced, while Sitaram quietly retrieves letters, destroys one, and lets Udayaditya be carried by boat to Raigarh, so the fire becomes not merely a distraction but a staged scene concealing the escape.

In his own court, Ramchandra Ray does not regard Udayaditya’s rescue as a favor to be thanked; he treats it as something that should have happened and believes Udayaditya acted mainly to protect his sister, so he joins in mocking Udayaditya rather than showing gratitude.

It is turned into a forged petition purporting to be from Udayaditya/Yubaraj to the Emperor—stamped with the prince's seal and delivered to Pratapaditya as intercepted evidence of treason—providing the pretext for imprisoning him.

The grooming of Vibha’s hair marks Surma’s presence through the intimate act of Surma doing Vibha’s hair to Vibha’s liking in the Jessore palace. After Surma’s tragic absence, the same ritual becomes a sign of loss: Vibha sits waiting for Surma to braid her hair, but Surma does not come, leaving Vibha’s hair unbraided and unkempt, so the absent or unstyled hair registers the painful fact that Surma is no longer there.
